title: Proxy
objectives: Use a substitute with the same service interface.
Trace lazy construction, cache hits, and invalidation.
Keep permission checks ahead of cached results.

sections.heading: A cheap question can trigger expensive work
paragraphs: A visitor display asks for a building's opening hour. In a real system that answer may require opening a connection or reading a remote schedule. This example uses a tiny in-memory Source so the behavior is deterministic. The source hour starts at eight, and a reads counter records real-service requests. The interface accepts hours already supplied by a trusted source; it does not validate a full calendar or time zone.

The simplest caller invokes the real service every time. That is appropriate when the service is cheap and fresh data matters more than reuse. The new requirements are to avoid creating the real service until needed, reuse the most recently fetched hour until told it is stale, and deny reads when local permission has been revoked. Repeating those rules at every caller would spread state management and make it easy to return a cached value after access was removed.

sections.heading: Use the same interface with an access-controlling substitute
paragraphs: A proxy is a substitute object that controls access to another service while offering the same interface. Hours defines opening(). RealHours reads Source and increments its reads counter. HoursProxy also implements opening, but it checks permission, checks its cache, creates RealHours if necessary, and calls it only when a fresh value is needed. Code written against Hours can use either object.

The proxy holds a Source reference and an optional unique_ptr<RealHours>. The pointer starts empty. Constructing the proxy therefore does not construct RealHours. Creating the real object only on first demand is called lazy initialization. Once created, the real service remains owned by the proxy even if cached data is invalidated. The two states answer different questions: is a service object present, and is there a remembered result?

Caching means retaining a result for later reuse. std::optional<int> stores either no value or one integer. It is a better representation than using zero as an empty marker because midnight, hour zero, is valid. Testing cached_ asks whether a value exists; it does not ask whether the stored integer is nonzero. Dereferencing it with *cached_ reads that value only after the program knows it is present.

sections.heading: Permission comes before the fast path
paragraphs: opening first checks allowed_. If false, it throws runtime_error immediately. It does this before consulting cached_. Revoking permission must stop both real-service reads and returns of data fetched earlier. A misplaced permission check after the cache hit would deny new reads but still expose old cached data. That is a precise ordering bug, not a reason to abandon caching.

This Boolean permission is a local teaching model, not an authentication system. There is no user identity, secret, network enforcement, or protection against a caller directly using RealHours. In a real application, access decisions need an authoritative policy and a boundary that unauthorized callers cannot bypass. The pattern explains where a check can sit; it does not make the check trustworthy by itself.

After permission succeeds, an engaged cache returns immediately without creating or reading a real service. On a cache miss, the proxy creates RealHours only if real_ is still empty. Then it calls real_->opening, stores the returned integer in cached_, and returns it. The virtual interface is the same, but allowed caching deliberately changes freshness. That semantic difference must be part of the service contract a caller accepts.

sections.heading: Trace old data and explicit invalidation
paragraphs: The first opening call sees no cache and no real service. It creates RealHours, reads eight, stores eight, and leaves source.reads equal to one. main changes source.hour to nine. The next opening call still returns eight, and the read counter stays one. That stale value is expected under this cache policy. Stale means no longer known to match the current source.

invalidate calls cached_.reset(), which removes the stored result but leaves real_ alive. The next permitted opening call reuses the already-created service object, reads nine, stores it, and advances reads to two. main then denies access and confirms that even this warm cache cannot be read. After re-enabling access, it changes the source to zero, invalidates, and calls twice. Both calls return zero, but only the first reads the source, leaving the final counter at three.

An invalidation policy says when remembered data stops being usable. This program makes that decision explicit in main. It does not watch Source automatically. A production design might attach a revision number, receive a change notification, use a maximum age, or always fetch fresh data for critical operations. Each choice has a cost and a freshness promise. A cache without a stated invalidation policy is an unfinished design.

sections.heading: Object lifetime and failure state
paragraphs: main creates Source before HoursProxy, so the borrowed source outlives the proxy. The proxy owns its RealHours through unique_ptr. RealHours itself borrows the same Source. Destroying the proxy destroys the optional cache and the real-service owner, but it does not destroy Source. Local declaration order supplies the required lifetime arrangement without manual deletion.

At compilation, override checks that both classes implement Hours::opening. The method is not const because obtaining an answer may change the cache and the source's diagnostic counter. A logically read-only business operation can still mutate implementation state; the interface should state that honestly rather than adding mutable everywhere without discussing consequences.

If allocation of RealHours fails, the owner remains empty and the cache remains empty. If a future real-service call throws before returning an integer, assignment to cached_ is not reached, so a miss remains uncached. The example's real service does not throw, but placing assignment after a successful call naturally avoids remembering a fabricated success. The exact state of a real service after its own failure would still depend on that service's contract.

The program is single-threaded. Concurrent calls could race while creating real_, reading Source, or changing cached_. shared ownership or virtual functions would not fix those races. A concurrent version would need synchronization and a clear rule for the order of revocation, invalidation, and in-flight requests. We do not add those mechanisms without the requirement because they would obscure the state transitions being taught.

Hours defaults construction but explicitly deletes copy and move operations. The = delete declarations make service objects stable in place; callers transfer an owning unique_ptr handle when ownership must change. Without this rule, an implicit proxy move would transfer real_ while leaving copied scalar cache and permission state in the source, creating two surprising service identities. Preventing object moves keeps the lifecycle contract simpler. Static type-trait checks verify that HoursProxy is neither copy-constructible nor move-constructible.

sections.heading: Distinguish the purpose of similar wrappers
paragraphs: Proxy and Decorator can both implement an interface and contain another implementation. A decorator normally adds independently selectable behavior to a component. A proxy stands in for a service to control access, location, or lifecycle. Our proxy creates its own real service on demand and manages a freshness policy. A diagram alone cannot settle which intent best describes a design; the requirements explain it.

For an inexpensive local value, directly reading Source may be simpler than either wrapper. For a service used exactly once, caching may add memory and complexity without avoiding work. Measure actual request patterns before optimizing. When a proxy is useful, expose enough diagnostics to test the behavior. The reads counter and loaded query let the example verify avoided work rather than merely checking that the printed hour looks right.

focus.title: Protect every path to a result
focus.what: The proxy rejects denied access before returning even a remembered value.
focus.where: This block is the first part of opening.
focus.why: A fast cache path must not bypass the permission contract.
focus.invariant: Every returned result follows a successful permission check.
focus.risk: Checking permission only on misses leaks cached data after revocation.
explain: The comment states the ordering rule.
Test whether access is currently denied.
Give the denial message and complete the throw.
Return the stored integer only if an optional value exists.

focus.title: Create once, fetch on misses
focus.what: A permitted miss creates the real service if needed, then stores a fetched result.
focus.where: This block runs only when permission succeeded and the cache was empty.
focus.why: Lazy construction avoids unused service objects, while caching avoids repeated reads.
focus.invariant: The cache is assigned only after the real call returns successfully.
focus.risk: Concurrent misses need synchronization; the current example is single-threaded.
explain: Check whether the real-service owner is empty.
Begin assigning a newly created owner.
Construct a RealHours object with make_unique.
Pass the borrowed source to its constructor.
Close the creation branch; an existing object is reused.
Fetch a value and engage the optional cache.
Close the miss path and opening method.

trace.reason: The first permitted miss creates and calls RealHours.
A hit follows the explicit cache policy.
The next miss fetches fresh source data.
The warm cache does not bypass access control.
An engaged optional can hold zero without another fetch.

summary: A proxy keeps the service interface while controlling access or lifecycle.
Lazy construction and cached results are separate states.
Check permission before any cached return.
Use optional when zero is a valid result.
Freshness requires an explicit invalidation policy.
A single-threaded proxy does not imply concurrent safety.

exercises.prompt: Set source.hour to seven before the first permitted opening call. What should the first result and read count be?
exercises.hint: The proxy has not fetched a value at construction.
exercises.answer: The first result is seven and reads is one. Constructing the proxy stores a source reference but does not snapshot its value or create the service.

exercises.prompt: Starting with a new Source and proxy, call opening twice, set source.hour=11, call opening, invalidate, then call opening. List the four results and final reads.
exercises.answer: The results are 8, 8, 8, and 11. Final reads is two. The source update alone does not clear cached eight; explicit invalidation causes the second real read.

exercises.prompt: A developer uses an int cached_=0 and considers zero an empty cache. What happens when opening hour is midnight and the caller asks three times?
exercises.hint: Midnight is a valid numeric result.
exercises.answer: All three calls are treated as misses and may trigger three source reads. The value cannot distinguish empty from midnight. Use optional<int> or a separate valid flag with a clear invariant.

exercises.prompt: A safety display requires the current source value on every request and the service is cheap. Should it use this cache policy?
exercises.answer: No. Use direct service calls or a proxy that checks permission but always fetches. Reusing an old value violates that display requirement, even if it improves speed. A maximum-age policy is appropriate only if the requirement permits that amount of staleness.

exercises.prompt: Add a test that denial before the first call leaves loaded() false and reads zero. Then allow and call again. State all expected observations.
exercises.hint: Denied access should stop before lazy construction.
exercises.answer: After allow(false), opening throws; loaded remains false and reads remains zero. After allow(true), opening returns eight, loaded becomes true, and reads becomes one. This catches construction performed unnecessarily before permission checking.

exercises.prompt: Explain to a teammate why invalidate does not destroy RealHours. Give a case where closing the real service as well could be reasonable.
exercises.hint: A stale result and an unusable connection are different conditions.
exercises.answer: The cached hour may be old while the service object is still useful for another read. Keeping it avoids reconstructing the connection. If a failed or revoked session makes the real service unusable, an explicit reset operation may clear both owner and cache, with separate tests for reconnection.

glossary.definition: A substitute service object that controls access, location, or lifecycle while keeping the service interface.
Creating an object only when it is first needed.
A request answered from an already stored result.
Declaring a remembered result unusable so a later request must fetch again.
Remembered data that is no longer known to match the current source.

example.title: A lazy cached opening-hour service
requirements: Do not create RealHours until the first permitted cache miss.
Reuse cached values until explicit invalidation.
Deny both cached and uncached reads when permission is false.
Treat hour zero as a real cached value.
example.design: One proxy keeps permission, lazy ownership, and cache state beside the service access they control. optional distinguishes no result from a valid zero result.
example.alternative: Direct service calls are simpler when freshness is always required or calls are cheap. A standalone caching function may fit one caller; a proxy fits interchangeable Hours users.
invariants: Denied reads never reach the service or return cached data.
An engaged cache contains a successful prior result.
Invalidation removes the result but does not destroy the service.
Source outlives the proxy and its real service.

failures.mistake: Use if (*cached_) to decide whether the cache contains data.
failures.consequence: Dereferencing an empty optional is invalid; zero is also incorrectly treated as a miss.
failures.reason: Value presence and numeric truth are different questions.

failures.mistake: Return cached data before checking allowed_.
failures.consequence: After revocation the caller still receives nine from the warm cache.
failures.reason: The fast path bypasses the permission rule.

failures.mistake: Assume changing source.hour refreshes the proxy automatically.
failures.consequence: After changing eight to nine, the next call returns eight.
failures.reason: No observer or revision check connects the source change to cache invalidation.

example.verification: Checks verify initial unloaded state, first-read construction, reuse without extra reads, stale behavior, explicit refresh after invalidation, denial with a warm cache, and cached zero. They do not test network access, real authentication, or concurrent execution. Compile-time type traits also verify that HoursProxy object copying and moving are disabled.
example.maintenance: A useful proxy must document freshness, access checks, and failure behavior as carefully as its interface. Test the work it avoids and the states it preserves.

diagram.title: HoursProxy controls access to the Hours service

nodes.label: Real Subject: RealHours
code: // Create once on a permitted miss.

diagram.explanation: The solid arrows show the miss path. The cache block returns directly on a hit, and the permission block throws directly on denial. The RealHours owner is created only if absent. invalidate clears cached_, sending the next permitted call back through the miss path; it leaves real_ intact.

lab.task: Add HoursProxy::refresh(), which forces a new successful read when access is allowed. A denied refresh must throw without clearing the current cache, creating a service, or reading Source. Keep every original behavior and test.
checks: After source changes to ten, refresh returns ten and increments reads once.
A denied refresh throws and leaves reads unchanged.
After denial, change source to eleven and re-allow access: opening still returns cached ten.
An allowed refresh then returns eleven.
lab.answer: The solution checks permission before invalidating, then calls opening to reuse the ordinary lazy-fetch path. Checking only inside opening after invalidation would erase valid cached state on a denied request, violating the lab requirement. Repeated permission checking is small and keeps the existing opening contract unchanged; a factored private permission helper is a reasonable cleanup.

problem_title: Control access to a service and know when cached data is old

attachment_alignment.intent: Control access to a service while preserving the operation callers already know. The attached EPUB discusses expensive creation, permission checks, cached results, logging, and remote services. These are different reasons to put a stand-in between a client and a real object. A particular Proxy must state which reason it serves and what callers may observe.
attachment_alignment.mechanism: Subject declares a common service interface. RealSubject performs the underlying work. Proxy implements that interface and decides whether to delegate, reject, reuse a result, or prepare the real service first. Client code can call either through Subject. The common C++ signature permits substitution, but the behavioral contract must also describe failures, freshness, and any other visible change.

roles.responsibility: Declare the operation clients use for both the service and its stand-in.
Perform the actual work when the proxy chooses to delegate.
Enforce access, creation, and caching policy around that work.
Request the service operation without repeating the proxy policy.

roles.role: Backing data, outside the pattern roles
roles.responsibility: Supply a changing hour and read counter so delegation is observable.

attachment_alignment.source_walkthrough: ClientCode first receives RealSubject and prints RealSubject: Handling request. main then constructs Proxy(real_subject). The constructor allocates a copy with new RealSubject(*real_subject); it does not borrow the original pointer and does not defer creation. ClientCode receives that Proxy through Subject. Request calls CheckAccess, which prints the access line and always returns true in this demonstration. The proxy then calls its owned copy’s Request and finally LogAccess, producing access, real request, and logging lines in that order. main deletes the original real_subject and the proxy separately; the proxy destructor deletes its private copy. Lazy creation and caching are mentioned as uses but are not implemented in this supplied C++ sample.
attachment_alignment.adaptation: HoursProxy makes three policies visible: lazy creation, a cached answer, and an access gate checked on every call. Initially no RealHours exists. The first permitted call creates it, reads 8, and caches that value. Changing Source to 9 does not change the next cached answer; invalidate makes the following call read 9. Revoking permission blocks even a cached answer, preventing a cache-hit bypass. The source sample’s logging and copied RealSubject are omitted. Our proxy instead owns one lazily constructed RealHours with unique_ptr and borrows Source; the source must outlive both. optional<int> distinguishes an absent answer from the valid hour zero. Hours has a virtual destructor for safe polymorphic destruction, unlike the attached Subject declaration. The single Boolean gate is a deterministic teaching policy, not a production identity or authorization system.
attachment_alignment.recognize: Find an object with the service interface that controls whether and when the real service is used. Ask what happens on a denied call, first call, repeated call, and invalidated call. A shared interface alone is not enough. Cached results need a stated freshness rule, and a remote proxy would additionally need an explicit network failure contract.

contrast.distinction: Decorator assembles optional behavior around components. Proxy represents a service and controls access or lifecycle; our cache and permission decisions determine whether the real call occurs.
Adapter changes an incompatible interface or meaning into the required contract. HoursProxy and RealHours already implement the same Hours interface.
Facade supplies a simpler task entrance to several subsystem operations. Proxy stands in for the service at its existing interface.

teach.action: List expensive first use, repeated reads, and revoked access. Decide which are requirements before introducing the proxy class.
Follow CheckAccess, the private RealSubject copy, and LogAccess. Point out that the supplied access test cannot currently deny a request.
Track loaded(), Source::reads, cached_, and allowed_ through a miss, a hit, invalidation, and denial. Explain the exact result of each path.
Implement refresh in the lab. Require permission before clearing the old cache or reading the source, and preserve the original miss and hit tests.

checks.question: Why must the access check happen before returning cached_?
checks.answer: Permission may have been revoked since the cache was filled. Returning the cached value first would bypass the new policy.

checks.question: Does the attached Proxy lazily create its RealSubject when Request is first called?
checks.answer: No. It creates an owned copy in its constructor. Our HoursProxy adds lazy creation explicitly and tests that no service exists before first permitted use.
